questions.q: What does a backup job reporting "completed successfully" actually confirm?
options: That the backup process ran without error, not that the data can actually be restored
That the backup has already been test-restored and verified
That the backup will never become corrupted in the future
That the RPO for that resource has been met permanently
questions.explain: Job success only means the backup process didn't error out — it doesn't verify the resulting backup is actually restorable.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a real, common cause of disaster-recovery failures?
options: Discovering a backup is corrupted or incomplete only when you desperately need it during a real incident
Taking backups too frequently and running out of storage
Using AWS Backup instead of Azure Backup
Setting an RTO that is too short to be realistic
questions.explain: A backup can silently fail to be restorable for a long time; the failure is only discovered at the worst possible moment unless it's tested first.

questions.q: What does a restore test actually involve?
options: Actually restoring a backup into a real (usually non-production) environment and verifying the result works
Checking that the backup job's log shows no errors
Increasing the retention period for all backups
Deleting old backups to save storage cost
questions.explain: A restore test means performing an actual restore and confirming the system comes up and the data is correct and current — not just reading a success log.

questions.q: How often does this lesson suggest restore testing should happen for a smaller environment?
options: On a defined, recurring cadence (quarterly as a common baseline), and after any significant configuration change
Only once, when the backup policy is first configured
Only after a real disaster has already occurred
Never, as long as the backup job reports success
questions.explain: Restore testing needs a real, recurring schedule plus a re-test after any significant change to what's being backed up.

questions.q: Why do teams often skip restore testing even when they configure backups diligently?
options: Restore testing is ongoing discipline with no visible urgency until the moment it's the only thing that matters
Restore testing is technically impossible in Azure or AWS
Backup jobs automatically perform restore tests on their own
Restore testing is only relevant for on-premises environments
questions.explain: Configuring backups is a one-time setup task, while proving a restore works is ongoing discipline — easy to defer until it's urgently needed.
